segments.text: [style: brisk, clear, architectural voice; steady studio cadence] Book Three, Proposition One. To find the center of a given circle. Let A B C be the given circle; it is required to find the center of the circle A B C.

subsegments.text: [style: brisk, clear, architectural voice; steady studio cadence] Book Three, Proposition One. To find the center of a given circle. Let A B C be the given circle; it is required to find the center of the circle A B C.

segments.style: speaking briskly, nimble, crisp, and composed
segments.text: [style: methodical, precise constructive cadence] Draw a chord A B through the circle at random, and bisect it at D by One Ten. From D, draw D C at right angles to A B, draw it through to E, and bisect C E at F. I say that F is the center. For suppose it is not, but, if possible, let G be the center, and join G A, G D, and G B.

subsegments.text: [style: methodical, precise constructive cadence] Draw a chord A B through the circle at random, and bisect it at D by One Ten. From D, draw D C at right angles to A B, draw it through to E, and bisect C E at F. I say that F is the center. For suppose it is not, but, if possible, let G be the center, and join G A, G D, and G B.

segments.style: speaking briskly, nimble, crisp, and composed
segments.text: [style: luminous, deductive geometric clarity] Because A D equals D B, D G is common, and the radii G A and G B are equal, by One Eight the adjacent angles A D G and G D B are equal, so angle G D B is a right angle by Definition Ten. Yet angle F D B is also a right angle by construction, making angle F D B equal to angle G D B, the greater to the less—which is impossible. Thus G is not the center, nor is any other point except F. Therefore F is the center of the circle A B C. Which was to be done.

segments.text: [style: reflective, scholarly, architectural synthesis] Proposition Three One opens Euclid's geometry of the circle, along with its celebrated Porism: the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the center. As Simson observed, because only the definition of a circle is available at the outset of Book Three, the proof must proceed by reductio ad absurdum. In the GEOMETOR G-Index, node G ninety-eight unites segment bisection and perpendicularity with Side-Side-Side congruence, becoming the constructive anchor for forty-four downstream theorems across Books Three, Four, Six, Twelve, and Thirteen.
